source.name: U.S. Census Bureau, Population Division Working Paper No. 81: Historical Census Statistics on the Foreign-Born Population of the United States: 1850 to 2000 (Campbell Gibson and Kay Jung, February 2006; successor to Working Paper No. 29, 1850-1990)
source.table: Table 14. Nativity of the Population, for Regions, Divisions, and States: 1850 to 2000 (states); Table 1. Nativity of the Population and Place of Birth of the Native Population: 1850 to 2000 (U.S.)

usSource.table: Table 1. Nativity of the Population and Place of Birth of the Native Population: 1850 to 2000

definition: "The native population includes all U.S. residents who were born in the United States or an outlying area of the United States (e.g., Puerto Rico), or who were born in a foreign country, but who had at least one parent who was an American citizen. All other residents of the United States are classified as foreign born." (Working Paper No. 81, text for Table 1). The paper notes the parent-citizen rule was introduced in 1890; before that, anyone born in a foreign country was foreign born.
notes: pct is the foreign-born percent of the total population, as published to one decimal. (The 2000 percentages are stored unrounded inside the Census spreadsheet; they are rounded here to one decimal, as printed in the paper.)

null means the Census table gives no figure: '(X)' not applicable (Alaska and Hawaii before 1960), '(NA)' not available (area not enumerated, e.g. Oklahoma before 1890), or the area is counted with another state.

North Dakota 1860-1880 is null because the figures shown for South Dakota are for the whole Dakota Territory (both Dakotas). West Virginia 1850-1860 is null because Virginia's figures include it. Oklahoma 1900 includes Oklahoma Territory and the Indian Territory.
1850 and 1860: nativity was not collected for enslaved people; the Census assumes, as the 1870 reports did, that all were native.
1890 excludes the population of Indian Territory and Indian reservations, for whom nativity was not collected. U.S. figures include Alaska and Hawaii from 1960.

The two Census tables differ slightly for 1960: Table 1 gives 9,738,091 foreign born for the U.S., Table 14 gives 9,738,143 (its U.S. line and its states add to 9,738,143). 'us' uses Table 1; 'states' use Table 14. Every other year agrees.
1950-2000 figures marked '*' by the Census are based on sample data.
